channel.title: Thirsty Planet
channel.description: Understanding water, before it's gone. The hidden water inside everyday things, the water industry in plain words, and the places already solving it.

item.title: Plain Water: Arsenic
item.description:
Bangladesh has the largest mass poisoning in history, and it was caused by a public health success.
In the 1970s and 1980s, aid agencies and the government sank millions of hand pumped tube wells across the country, to replace the pond and river water that spread cholera and killed children by the hundred thousand. The wells worked. Child mortality fell. Nobody tested the water for arsenic, because nobody thought to, and the sediments of the Ganges delta, laid down from the Himalayas over thousands of years, release arsenic into the groundwater at levels far above anything safe.
The poisoning is slow. Skin lesions appear after years, then cancers of the skin, lung and bladder after decades. Around twenty million people in Bangladesh still drink water above the country's own limit, and the WHO guideline is five times stricter than that. I have spent time in Bangladesh, and the painted wells, red for unsafe and green for safe, are the most sobering piece of water infrastructure I know.
Filters work, deeper wells work, and rain and treated surface water work. What has been slow is the money and the attention.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Antiscalants
item.description:
Every reverse osmosis plant has a small tank of chemical beside the pumps, dosed at a few milligrams per litre, without which the plant would stop within days. It is called an antiscalant, and it is the least known critical chemical in the water business.
The problem it solves is the kettle's problem, at pressure. A membrane concentrates everything it rejects, and on the brine side of the membrane the calcium, sulphate and bicarbonate that were comfortably dissolved in the feed are pushed several times past the point at which they would come out of solution. They crystallise, on the membrane surface, as scale, and scale blocks the membrane the way it furs a kettle element.
An antiscalant is a molecule, usually a phosphonate or a polymer, that sits on the surface of a forming crystal and stops it growing. It does not remove the hardness. It persuades the hardness to stay dissolved a little longer than chemistry says it should, long enough to leave with the brine.
Get the dose right and the membranes last seven years. Get it wrong and they last a season. The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Myth: Water Can't Run Out
item.description:
The water cycle is true. The amount of water on Earth is fixed, it has been the same for billions of years, and every drop that evaporates comes down again somewhere. From that, most people conclude that water cannot run out, and it is the most comforting mistake in the subject.
Water itself never runs out. Fresh water does: fresh water in a particular place, at a particular time, clean enough to use. The rain over the ocean is no use to a farm. The rain in a monsoon week is no use in the dry season unless something stored it. And the water under the ground, which is what half the world's irrigation now pumps, is in many places older than farming, laid down in wetter ages thousands of years ago, and refilled at a rate that has nothing to do with how fast it is being spent. The Ogallala under the American plains, the aquifers of north west India, the Nubian sandstone under the Sahara: these are being mined, and the satellites that weigh the Earth's water can watch them fall.
The cycle is real. The bank account is local, and some of the accounts are being emptied.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Myth: Rain Is Pure Water
item.description:
Rain is the purest water most people will ever see. It has been evaporated by the sun, which leaves every salt and mineral behind, and it comes down with about ten milligrams of dissolved solids in a litre, against a few hundred in tap water. That is the true half of the myth.
The other half is what rain meets on the way down and where it lands. Every drop forms on a speck of dust, it washes the air of soot, pollen, sulphur and, we now know, PFAS, at levels that exceed the new drinking water limits nearly everywhere on Earth. Then it hits a roof, with its bird droppings, its moss, its lead flashing and its zinc, and runs into a gutter and a barrel, where the last of the story is written by whatever grows in the dark.
Rain is excellent water to harvest, and Chennai, Bermuda and half of rural Australia run on it. It is water to be filtered and disinfected like any other, and the sense in which it is pure is the sense that matters least to a stomach.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Myth: Flushable wipes are flushable
item.description:
"Flushable wipes are flushable." The packet says so, the wipe goes down, and the sewer disagrees.
A flush proves nothing. Almost anything small enough will leave a toilet bowl. The question is what happens in the pipe, and the answer for most wet wipes is that nothing happens. Toilet paper is made to fall apart in water within seconds. A wipe is a nonwoven fabric, often bonded with plastic fibres, made to stay in one piece while wet, which is its whole purpose and its whole problem.
In the sewer, wipes snag, collect, and bind with the cooking fat that also should not be there, into masses that block pipes and pumps. The largest of these, found under Whitechapel in London in 2017, weighed 130 tonnes and stretched 250 metres. Britain's water companies clear around 300,000 sewer blockages a year and say most are wipes and fat.
The industry's verdict is plain: toilets are for the two things the body produces and paper. Everything else goes in the bin, whatever the packet says.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Myth: Boiling water removes everything
item.description:
"If in doubt, boil it." Good advice, and it covers half of what can be wrong with water.
Boiling kills. One minute at a rolling boil, three at altitude, and every bacterium, virus and parasite in the water is dead, including the Cryptosporidium that chlorine cannot touch. That is why a boil water notice is the right response to a burst main or a failed filter, and why boiling has saved more lives than any other water treatment in history.
Boiling does not remove anything. Salt, nitrate, lead, arsenic, pesticides, the fluoride in the tap and the dissolved solids that make the kettle fur: all of it stays in the pan, and since some of the water leaves as steam, what remains is slightly more concentrated than before. The scale in the kettle is the proof. It is the dissolved minerals, made visible by the heat, and none of them went anywhere.
Two problems, two tools. Microbes: boil. Chemistry: a filter, a membrane, or a different source. The kettle only ever solved the first.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Myth: A bath uses more water than a shower
item.description:
"A shower uses less water than a bath." It depends, and the modern shower has quietly overturned the rule.
A full standard bath holds about 80 litres, and a large one 150. A typical shower head delivers 8 to 10 litres a minute, so a five minute shower is 40 to 50 litres and a bath wins by nothing. A power shower delivers 15 litres a minute or more, and ten minutes under one is 150 litres, a large bath. The average shower in Britain lasts seven to eight minutes, which puts it, at a typical head, level with a bath.
The line is easy to find. Time the shower, put a bucket under the head for a minute to measure the flow, and multiply. Under 80 litres and the shower wins. Over it and the bath was the economical choice all along.
The water is the smaller half of it. Heating that water is the largest energy use in most homes after the heating itself, and every litre of hot water, bath or shower, was heated by gas or electricity.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Wine
item.description:
Almost every farmer on Earth is trying to get more water to their crop. Winemakers are the strange exception. They spend their careers trying to make the plant a little thirsty.
A vine with plenty of water grows big, watery grapes and lots of leaves. A vine that has to work sends its roots down and produces small grapes with concentrated flavour, which is what ends up tasting like something. Growers call the technique deficit irrigation, and in parts of Europe the rules go further: several famous appellations simply forbid irrigation, on the grounds that a vineyard that needs watering is planted in the wrong place.
All of which makes the number a little awkward. A glass of wine still carries about 109 litres of water, and per litre wine costs roughly three times what beer does. Grapes are not especially thirsty; there just are not many of them per bottle, and the vine drinks rain all season either way.
The part worth watching is what heat is doing to those old rules. Regions that built their identity on never irrigating are facing summers their vines were not planted for, and some of the bans have quietly started to bend.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Avocado
item.description:
This series has spent a lot of posts arguing that a big water number is not automatically bad news. Chocolate drinks tropical rain. Coffee mostly does too. The avocado is where that argument stops.
The difference is where the water comes from. Cocoa trees stand in some of the wettest places on Earth and drink what falls on them. Avocados prefer dry Mediterranean climates, which means Chile, Spain, Mexico, California, and in those places the water arrives through a pipe. Someone pumped it out of a river or a well, and it was not available for anything else afterwards.
Petorca in Chile is the case everyone in the water world knows. A fruit growing province where plantations expanded fast, rivers ran low, and residents ended up receiving drinking water by tanker truck while orchards nearby stayed green. That is a truck in a village rather than a footprint calculation.
None of which makes avocados forbidden. It makes them the fruit where origin actually matters, and the sticker on the skin says more about water than any number on a chart.
The long version, with the fruit table and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: TDS
item.description:
Pick up a bottle of mineral water and look near the bottom of the label. There will be a line saying dry residue at 180 degrees, followed by a number. That number is TDS, total dissolved solids, and once you know it you will read water differently.
It is everything dissolved into the water: salt, calcium, magnesium, whatever the water met on its way through the ground. Rain has almost none. Tap water runs a few hundred milligrams per litre. Seawater sits around 35,000.
Two things follow. The first is that TDS is what water tastes like. Water with nothing in it tastes flat, which is why distilled water is unpleasant and why mineral water brands advertise their minerals instead of hiding them. The second is that dissolved is the hard problem in my industry. A filter catches things by being too small to let them through, and dissolved salt has come apart into pieces far smaller than any pore. You cannot strain it, settle it, or feed it to bacteria. The only ways out are a membrane at very high pressure, boiling, or a resin, and all three cost energy. That is why salt is the wall every water recycling project eventually hits.
The long version, with the scale, the measurement and the three ways out, is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Strawberries
item.description:
A punnet of strawberries carries about 140 litres of water, which is not much, and the strawberries in a northern supermarket in February carry a story that is. They were picked in Huelva, in the south west of Spain, which grows most of Spain's strawberries and sends Europe its winter berries, under thousands of hectares of plastic tunnels, on water pumped from an aquifer that also feeds Doñana, the largest wetland in western Europe.
A strawberry plant has shallow roots and a fruit that is nine tenths water, and grown out of season under plastic it is watered by drip every day from a well. The wells in Huelva have multiplied for thirty years, a share of them without a permit, and the water table under the marshes has fallen. The lagoons that the flamingos and the migrating birds depend on have dried in summer, including ones that had never dried before.
In 2021 the European court ruled that Spain had failed to protect the aquifer. In 2023 the regional government tried to legalise the irrigation anyway, and backed down. The berries are still picked in February.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Montevideo
item.description:
Uruguay has more fresh water per person than almost any country on Earth, a river the width of a sea on its doorstep, and a capital that in June 2023 had about ten days of drinking water left. The Paso Severino reservoir on the Santa Lucía river, which supplies Montevideo and most of the country's people, fell below two percent after three years of drought, and the state did the only thing it could do quickly: it mixed what was left with water from the Río de la Plata, which is brackish, and raised the legal limit on salt in the tap water so the mix would be legal.
For two months the water in nearly two million taps was salty enough to taste, with sodium at more than double the usual limit. The health ministry told pregnant women, people with kidney disease and heart patients to drink bottled water, the government took the tax off it, and the supermarkets ran out. The protests carried a slogan that translates as "it is not drought, it is plunder", aimed at the farms and the pulp mills that take the rivers upstream.
The rain came in August. The city is now building a second source on the estuary, which is the sea with a river in it.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Dubai
item.description:
Dubai has no river, a hundred millimetres of rain in a good year, an aquifer that is brackish and nearly spent, and nearly four million people who use more water per head than almost anyone on Earth. Almost every drop they drink was the Gulf a day earlier. The plants at Jebel Ali, next to the power station, turn more than two million cubic metres of seawater a day into drinking water, and the city would have a few days of supply in its tanks if they stopped.
For forty years the plants boiled the sea with the waste heat of the gas turbines that make the city's electricity, which is why Dubai's water and its power have always come from the same company and the same fuel. The new plants push the water through membranes instead, with a third of the energy, run on solar electricity from the desert, and the last boiling plant is being retired.
The sewage goes to two works in the desert and comes back as the water on every verge, park and golf course in the city, and as the lagoon at the end of the creek where the flamingos stand. The storm of April 2024 showed what the city had never built: drains.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Bogotá
item.description:
Bogotá drinks from a moorland. Above the city, at three and four thousand metres, lies the páramo of Chingaza, a cold wet plateau of fog, moss and a plant called the frailejón that looks like a palm crossed with a cabbage, and whose soils hold water like a sponge and let it go slowly into the rivers. Seven tenths of the capital's water is collected there, in two reservoirs, and carried down through a tunnel in the mountain.
In early 2024 El Niño dried the páramo. The Chuza reservoir fell to about 16 percent, lower than it had ever been, and on 11 April the city began rationing: eight million people divided into nine zones, each cut off for 24 hours in turn. The rota ran, with changes, for a year. People filled bathtubs and buckets on the night before their day, the car washes closed, and the city's use fell by about a tenth and stayed down.
The rains returned, the reservoirs filled, and the rationing ended in April 2025. What it taught was that a city of eight million was one dry year from the tanks on the roofs of Amman.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Irrigation
item.description:
Of all the fresh water people take out of rivers, lakes and the ground, about seven tenths goes to one thing: watering crops. Industry takes about a fifth and every city, town and household on Earth takes the rest. Irrigation is the thirsty industry that the others on this site are footnotes to.
It covers about a fifth of the world's cropland and grows about two fifths of its food, and most of it is done the way it was done in Mesopotamia: water let onto a field through a gate and left to soak in. Half of that water never reaches a plant. Sprinklers and drip lines do better, and the countries that have switched to them have mostly grown more crops on the same water rather than giving any back, which is the paradox the engineers and the economists have argued over for twenty years.
A fifth of the world's irrigated land is damaged by the salt the water leaves behind. The aquifer under the American plains, which feeds the circles seen from every flight across the country, is going down by a metre a year in Kansas and Texas. The food on the table came from one of these fields.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Hospitals
item.description:
A hospital bed uses several hundred litres of water a day in a rich country, up to a thousand in the busiest sites, which is a small household's week. Hardly any of it is drunk. It goes into the steam sterilisers, the laundry, the cooling towers, the kitchens, the hundreds of basins at which hands are washed, and the one machine that is more particular about water than any other in the building.
A dialysis machine passes about 120 litres of water across a patient's blood in a session, three times a week, and that water has to be cleaner than drinking water by a wide margin. The chlorine and chloramine that keep city water safe to drink will destroy red blood cells if they reach the dialyser, so every dialysis unit runs its own small treatment plant: carbon to strip the chlorine, reverse osmosis to strip the rest, and a loop that is tested for bacteria and endotoxin because a fever in a dialysis ward is a water fault until proved otherwise.
What goes out carries antibiotics, contrast agents and the drugs of the oncology ward, and the plant that cleans the city's sewage was not designed for them.
The long version is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Banana
item.description:
A banana carries about a hundred litres of water. Most of it fell as rain on a plantation on the coast of Ecuador, which sends the world a third of the bananas it trades, or in the Philippines, Costa Rica, Colombia or Guatemala, and almost all of it went through the plant: a banana plant is a giant herb with no woody stem, and it moves water from the soil to the air faster than most trees.
Per kilogram the banana is one of the lighter footprints on this site, about 790 litres against 1,800 for a mango and 2,500 for rice, because the fruit is heavy and the plant grows fast where the rain is two metres a year. The water that matters is the smaller part: the irrigation on the dry coasts, the wash tanks of the packing station, and the forty flights a year of fungicide over the plantations of the wet countries.
Every export banana is the same plant, a clone called Cavendish, and a soil fungus that kills it has crossed from Asia to Latin America. The water will be the same for whatever replaces it.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Turbidity
item.description:
Hold a glass of water up to the light and the first thing you judge is whether you can see through it. The water industry turned that glance into a number: turbidity, measured by shining a light into the water and counting how much of it is scattered sideways by the particles it cannot pass through. The unit is the NTU, and a river in flood runs at hundreds; the water leaving a modern filter runs at a tenth.
The particles themselves, clay, silt, algae, are mostly harmless. The reason the number matters is what hides in them. A parasite like Cryptosporidium, which chlorine cannot kill, travels on and inside the particles, and a filter that lets the particles through lets the parasite through. In Milwaukee in 1993 the turbidity of the finished water rose for days, within the rules of the time, and 400,000 people fell ill. The rule in the United States is now 0.3 NTU, in 95 percent of samples, which is a cloudiness no eye can see.
The number on the plant's screen is the one the operator watches most. A rise of a few tenths is the first sign that a filter has broken through.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Septic Tanks
item.description:
About one American household in five is not on a sewer, and neither are a third of the people on Earth. The water that leaves the house goes into a buried tank in the garden, sits there for a day or two, and seeps out into the ground. Nothing on this site is older, cheaper, or more often ignored until it fails.
The tank does less than people think. The solids settle to the bottom and the grease floats, and the water in between leaves about as dirty as it came, a third cleaner at best. The real treatment is the soil under the drain field: a metre of unsaturated earth, alive with bacteria, that finishes the job the tank started before the water reaches the groundwater. A tank on clay, or on sand with the water table a few feet down, or next to the well that supplies the house, is a different story, and it is the story of the nitrate in a lot of private wells.
Multiply it by a suburb and the nitrogen reaches the bay. Cape Cod, Long Island and the Florida lagoons are learning what a hundred thousand tanks do to an estuary. The tank in the garden is a treatment plant, and almost nobody treats it as one.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Myth: Chlorine in Tap Water Is Dangerous
item.description:
Chlorine is a poison. It was used as a gas on the Western Front, a leak from a railway tanker empties a town, and a cylinder of it stands in a locked room at most of the water works in the world, from which a little is dosed into the water that comes out of your tap. The myth says that a chemical that dangerous cannot be safe to drink. The verdict is that at the dose in a glass of water it is among the safest things in the glass.
A tap carries a few tenths of a milligram of chlorine a litre. The World Health Organization's limit for a lifetime of drinking is five, and a swimming pool runs at one to three. At those doses chlorine has been studied for a century in more people than any other substance in water, and what the studies found is the opposite of the myth: when the cities of Europe and America began adding chlorine, from 1908 onward, typhoid and cholera went from the leading killers of children to diseases a doctor might never see.
The real argument is about the byproducts chlorine makes with the organic traces in water, which are regulated and which this site has covered. The chlorine itself is in the glass so that nothing else is.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterFacts #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Paper
item.description:
Every office email footer used to beg the same thing: please consider the environment before printing. That request was worth about 10 litres of water per sheet.
Most of it went through a tree. A plantation pine or eucalyptus drinks rain for years before it becomes pulp, and that patience is what the sheet inherits. The mill's share used to be enormous too, but this is one of industry's quiet success stories. A modern paper mill runs its water in loops and uses about a tenth of what mills used decades ago. The machines improved. The tree still takes its time.
The everyday scale is what makes paper interesting. One sheet is nothing. A ream is 5,000 litres. An office printer that runs through a box of paper a week is quietly moving a swimming pool through it every few months. And the recycled sheet in the same tray skips the tree entirely, which roughly halves the whole number.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Food and beverage
item.description:
Cook one dinner and look at the sink afterwards. The colander, the pans, the board covered in potato peel, the water going brown in the bowl. That is a food factory, except it never stops and it handles tonnes an hour.
Food and beverage is a bigger industry than most people picture. Dairies, breweries, bottling plants, bakeries, meat plants, canneries, sugar mills. In Europe it is the largest manufacturing sector there is, and one of the heaviest industrial users of water anywhere.
The strange part is that most of that water never touches the food. Somewhere between half and two thirds of it goes on cleaning the equipment. A crisp factory washes its potatoes, steam peels them, slices them, rinses off the starch, fries, cools, and at the end of the shift washes down the whole line. A dairy pushes hot water and detergent through its own pipework between every batch, and in some plants that cleaning uses more water than the milk it processed.
Nobody can simply wash less. When the product is food, hygiene is not a place to economise. So the industry got clever in another direction: water used in order, cleanest job first, dirtiest last, and the sugary, milky effluent at the end digested into biogas that heats the factory.
The long version, with the tables and the sources, is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: Sludge
item.description:
A wastewater plant does not make dirt disappear. Nothing does. What a plant actually does is sort: clean water goes out one way, and everything that was in it gets gathered into a single heap. That heap has a name, sludge, and it is the part of the industry nobody puts on the brochure.
Two things about it surprise people. The first is that fresh sludge is about 99 percent water. The plant then spends enormous effort squeezing it down to a cake that is roughly a quarter solids and still feels damp, so a good deal of the machinery in a treatment works exists to take water out of something that was just taken out of water. The second is the bill. Handling sludge can eat up to half of a plant's running costs.
There is a good story in it too. Digested in sealed tanks, sludge gives off biogas that plants burn for power, and what remains is full of nitrogen and phosphorus, which is exactly what farmland wants. The complication is that everything anyone pours down a drain ends up in the same heap, including the forever chemicals called PFAS, and in 2022 the state of Maine banned spreading sludge on farmland because of them.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Milk
item.description:
A litre of milk takes about 1,020 litres of water to produce. As with steak and eggs, the animal barely drinks any of it. The water is in the grass, hay and grain a dairy cow works through every day to keep giving milk.
The question this number always raises is about the alternatives. Counted by irrigation water in one large global study, dairy is the heaviest option per litre. Almond milk comes next, mostly because almonds grow in dry places on pumped water. Oat and soy sit far below both. Different studies count differently, so the figures move around, but the order stays fairly stable.
Worth adding before anyone clears out the fridge: per gram of protein, milk performs about as well as eggs and much better than beef. And a carton from cows grazing rain fed pasture tells a different story than one from a dry region herd eating irrigated feed. The average hides a lot.
The long version, with the tables and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Bread
item.description:
Bread rarely makes anyone's list of thirsty foods, which is exactly why it belongs on this one. A kilo of bread carries about 1,608 litres of water. Cut the loaf into slices and each one took roughly 65 litres, about the same as a seven minute shower.
Almost all of it is the wheat. Wheat is the largest crop on the planet by land area, a quiet carpet across Europe, the American plains, India, China and Russia. Around 70 percent of its water arrives as rain, which is the gentle kind. The concern sits in the other 30 percent. In parts of northern India and the Middle East, wheat runs on pumped groundwater, and the wells there have been dropping for decades. Same grain, very different sources.
Bread also makes the multiplication visible. One kilo is manageable. Humanity bakes hundreds of millions of tonnes of wheat into food every year, and every tonne carried its water with it.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Plain Water: ETP
item.description:
Next to almost every serious factory in the world there is a building most people never notice. Tanks, pipes, a smell of earth, a low hum. That building decides whether the river next door stays alive.
It is called an ETP, an effluent treatment plant, and inside the industry its nickname is the factory's kidney. Used water comes in carrying dye, oil, starch, salt, whatever the factory does for a living. The plant takes it out. The surprising part is how: the core of nearly every ETP is a large tank of bacteria that eat pollution as food. Operators feed them, keep them warm, and pump air into the water around the clock so they can breathe. Half or more of the plant's electricity goes on that air.
Which points at the real weakness. An ETP costs money every hour it runs and makes nothing anyone can sell. So in places with thin margins and thinner enforcement, plants get switched off between inspections. The technology was solved decades ago. Running it, honestly, every day, is the part the world is still working on.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: COD
item.description:
A strange fact from the water business: one of the worst things you can pour into a river is milk.
Not because it is toxic. Because of the number the industry uses to measure how dirty water is. It is called COD, chemical oxygen demand, and it is the amount of oxygen it would take to break down everything dissolved in a litre of water. Dirt in water is food. Microbes eat it and breathe oxygen from the water while they do, the same oxygen fish need. COD measures how much oxygen the dirt could take down with it.
A clean mountain stream has a COD of about 2 milligrams per litre. Raw sewage is around 500. Milk is roughly 200,000. A tanker of milk in a river is treated as a serious pollution emergency, and now you know why.
Every discharge permit sets a COD limit. Every treatment plant is judged by how much COD it removes. It is a load meter, not a poison meter, and that distinction is the whole art of reading it.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Plain Water: After you flush
item.description:
The flush is the last most people ever see of their water. From there it starts a trip that runs under every street in the city, powered mostly by gravity, all the way to a plant at the lowest point of town.
Two things about that plant surprise almost everyone. First, sewage is about 99.9 percent water. The whole system, the pipes, the tanks, the billions in infrastructure, exists to remove a fraction the size of a sugar cube in a bucket. Second, the plant runs on biology. The cleaning is done by tanks of bacteria that eat the dirt, and the dirt they remove is digested into biogas. The better plants power a large share of their own operations with it, which means a flush partly funds its own cleanup.
The number worth sitting with is global. By UN estimates more than 80 percent of the world's wastewater still returns to nature with no treatment at all. The technology is a century old. Most of humanity just does not have the plant yet.
The long version is on the site.
#WaterTreatment #Wastewater #WaterEducation #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Rice
item.description:
A flooded rice paddy looks like the crop must need to grow underwater. It does not. Rice grows fine in moist soil. The water is there mostly as weed control: rice tolerates standing water and weeds drown in it. Farmers have used that trick for thousands of years because it works and needs no chemicals.
The cost of the trick is scale. Rice feeds about half the world every day, and growing one kilo takes around 2,500 litres of water. Across Asia's paddies that adds up to roughly a third of all the irrigation water used on Earth, more than any other crop.
The interesting part is happening on farms right now. A method called alternate wetting and drying, where paddies are allowed to dry out for a few days before being flooded again, cuts water use by about a quarter without losing yield. It is low tech, it is spreading, and it is one of the biggest single water savings available anywhere.
The long version, with the numbers and the sources, is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty: Chocolate
item.description:
A 100 gram bar of chocolate takes about 1,700 litres of water to produce. Most people read that number twice.
The explanation is mostly the tree. Cocoa grows in the wettest parts of Ghana, Ivory Coast and Indonesia, drinks rain all year, and at the end of a season a single tree yields only a few kilos of beans. Then it takes a lot of beans to make a little chocolate. So each bar carries years of accumulated rainfall, around 17,000 litres per kilo, which on paper is more than beef.
Worth knowing before drawing conclusions: about 98 percent of that water is rain that fell on tropical farmland anyway. Cocoa is not draining rivers. Its actual problem is temperature. The belt where cocoa grows well keeps getting narrower as the climate warms, and the industry is already moving farms and breeding for heat because of it.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Beef
item.description:
A 200 gram steak carries about 3,100 litres of water, and nearly all of it was spent before the animal ever drank.
Cattle eat for roughly three years before slaughter: grass, hay, grain. Growing all that feed takes water every season, and when those years of feed water are divided by the meat one animal yields, beef lands around 15,400 litres per kilo, the highest of the common meats. The animal's own drinking water is about one percent of the total.
The number changes a great deal with how the animal was raised. Cattle on rain fed pasture mostly use rain that fell on grassland anyway. Cattle fed irrigated grain in a dry region draw on rivers and aquifers. The same steak on the plate, a very different water story behind it.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: The turn
item.description:
Every number posted in the first month of this series was spent before the product reached anyone. Coffee, 140 litres. A t-shirt, 2,700. A steak, 3,100. Jeans, 8,000. Read enough of those and it starts to feel like a personal accusation. It is not one.
Those litres were used in fields and factories, and factory water in particular has a property that changes everything: it is concentrated. A mill's wastewater leaves through one pipe, and whatever flows through one pipe can be measured, treated and sent back into the process. With equipment that already exists, 70 to 90 percent of industrial wastewater can be recovered. Plants doing exactly this run every day, quietly, on every continent.
The reason it is not standard everywhere is rarely technical: cost, and whether customers, regulators or neighbours are asking for it. Asking turns out to matter.
This is where the series turns: less "look how much water", more "look what can be done with it".
The long version is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty: T-shirt
item.description:
There is a sea missing in Central Asia, and part of the reason is hanging in your wardrobe.
The Aral Sea was once the fourth largest lake on Earth. From the 1960s the two rivers feeding it were diverted to irrigate cotton, and over a few decades most of it turned to desert. Fishing towns now sit a hundred kilometres from the water.
That is the uncomfortable thing about cotton. It is a natural fibre, it feels like the responsible choice, and it is also one of the thirstiest crops in farming. One t-shirt carries about 2,700 litres of water by the Water Footprint Network's method, roughly what one person drinks in three years. About 85 percent of it is the field.
The good news does not require shopping differently. It mostly requires keeping clothes longer. Every extra year a shirt stays in use, its water per wear shrinks.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.

item.title: Thirsty: Jeans
item.description:
The CEO of Levi's once told an audience he had not washed his jeans in a year. It sounded like a stunt. It was actually water policy.
His company had just finished one of the most detailed studies ever done on a single garment, and it found something unexpected: nearly a quarter of all the water a pair of jeans uses in its lifetime is spent in the owner's washing machine. The farm grows the cotton, the mill dyes it blue, and then the biggest saving left on the table belongs to whoever wears them.
The full farm to shop number is about 8,000 litres per pair, by the Water Footprint Network's method. Around 85 percent of it is the cotton field. The dye house, where the colour goes on and a good part of it comes straight back off in the rinse, is a distant second.
The long version, with the breakdown, the indigo chemistry and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #HiddenWater #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Industries: Textile
item.description:
Fashion withdraws 93 billion cubic metres of water a year. Almost all of it comes back, and that is the problem.
Textiles is an industry that consumes little water and discharges a lot of it: hot, alkaline, loaded with salt, and coloured by dye that never bonded to the fibre. Colour is the part people underestimate. Dye blocks light from reaching into a river, less light means less photosynthesis, and less photosynthesis means less oxygen for anything living in it.
I have stood inside the plants that deal with this water. Conventional wet processing uses 100 to 150 litres of water per kilo of fabric. The best run mills operate near 50, and the gap between those numbers is management, not new technology. Beyond that, a treatment plant followed by membranes can bring 70 to 90 percent of a mill's effluent back into the process.
Treatment does not make the pollution disappear, though. It concentrates it into two streams, a salty brine and a heap of sludge, and what a mill does with those two is now the real question in this industry.
The long version, with the effluent table, the dye house mechanism and the sources, is on the site.
#IndustrialWater #WaterTreatment #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Coffee
item.description:
By the time a cup of coffee reaches your kitchen, about 140 litres of water have already gone into it. The kettle adds a fraction of a litre. The rest was spent months earlier, on a hillside in Ethiopia, Brazil or Vietnam, while the beans were still on the tree.
The number comes from the Water Footprint Network method, which counts three kinds of water: the rain the crop drank, the irrigation it was given, and the water needed to dilute whatever it polluted. Per kilo of roasted coffee it comes to roughly 18,900 litres. A cup uses about seven grams, so 132 litres for the growing, a few more for processing, and the cup is done.
The part most people never hear is that a big number is not automatically bad news. Most coffee grows on rain, and rain on a tropical hillside was never going to come out of anyone's tap. The story changes when thirsty crops are grown in dry places on pumped water. So the useful question about coffee, and about most things you own, is whose water it was, and where it came from.
The full article, with the breakdown, the mechanism and the sources, is on the site.

item.title: The 0.3%
item.description:
Somewhere in school, everyone saw the photo of Earth from space and heard that 70 percent of the planet is water. True, and it hides the real story.
About 97.5 percent of Earth's water is salt. Of the small fraction that is fresh, most is frozen in ice sheets and glaciers or lies too deep underground to reach. The rivers and lakes that supply most of what people, farms and factories actually use hold about 0.3 percent of the freshwater, which is less than a hundredth of a percent of all the water on the planet.
The twist is that this small share never runs out. Rain brings it back every year. So why do cities go dry? Because water is the one resource that cannot be shipped around the planet. Oil goes on a tanker. A river stays where it is. One country has more than it knows what to do with, and another counts the days until the taps stop.
That is the story this series tells, one everyday object at a time. The long version is on the site.
#WaterFootprint #WaterEducation #Sustainability #Water

item.title: Thirsty Places: Singapore
item.description:
Singapore has almost no natural freshwater. So it built a national supply out of the water it had already used.
The country runs what it calls four national taps: rain caught across the island, water imported from Malaysia, desalinated seawater, and NEWater, which is treated used water clean enough to drink and able to meet up to 40 percent of national demand.
NEWater is microfiltration, then reverse osmosis, then ultraviolet disinfection. None of that is exotic. It is standard equipment, the same train a textile mill uses to recycle its effluent, run well and maintained properly. The engineering was the easy part.
Asking people to drink it took more work, and Singapore did it by showing the process instead of hiding it. Years of published testing before launch. A visitor centre where the membranes are behind glass. A prime minister drinking it on camera. A name that described the product rather than its past.
Most cities that have rejected water reuse had the same technology available. What they lacked was that conversation.
The long version, with the four taps, the process and the sources, is on the site.
#WaterScarcity #WaterManagement #Cities #Water

item.title: Thirsty: Beer
item.description:
How much water does it take to make a beer? Not the water in the glass. All of it: the barley in the field, the rain and irrigation months before the brewery, the brewing itself.
One 250 millilitre glass comes to about 74 litres by the Water Footprint Network's method, roughly 298 litres for every litre of beer. Around 92 percent of it grew the barley. The brewery is a rounding error on top.
The part I find genuinely hopeful is inside that rounding error. Making one litre of beer takes around four to seven litres of water in a conventional brewery, most of it for cleaning tanks and pipes between batches, and the best operations have pushed the figure below three. Brewing is one of the industries that measures its water hardest, because every litre saved is money, and the effluent, rich in sugar and yeast, is increasingly digested for biogas.
Same story as coffee. The water is real, it was just spent somewhere else.
The long version, with the breakdown and the sources, is on the site.

item.title: Plain Water: Wastewater
item.description:
Wastewater is not a dirty word, and it is not another word for sewage.
It is any water that has already been used, by a shower, a brewery, a farm, a street in the rain, and now carries something it did not carry before. Sewage is one kind of it. A factory's effluent is another. Runoff is a third. Using the words interchangeably is the most common mistake people make about my industry.
The part that surprises people: typical municipal wastewater is more than 99 percent plain water. The whole business of treatment exists for the last one percent, and that one percent is enough. Bacteria in a river eat the organic matter in it and use up the dissolved oxygen while they do. Fish suffocate long before the water ever looks dirty.
Almost nothing in wastewater is visible. It is dissolved. That is why the sector measures water rather than looking at it, and why the next terms in this series are all measurements.
The long version is on the site.
